name: Cold spoons

lead: Cold spoons are spoons chilled in the freezer or fridge and held against the skin around the eyes to reduce puffiness. People use them for a quick, temporary de-puff, such as in the morning.

Cold is said to narrow blood vessels and reduce fluid in the tissue for a short time, so the area looks flatter. A general reference describes cold compression as sometimes recommended for swelling, with mixed evidence. Only a thin forum discussion of the spoon method exists, and no studies have tested it.

paras: People chill a metal spoon, hold the back against the closed eye area for a minute or two, and swap to a second spoon as the first warms. It is used as a morning routine step before skincare or makeup.
Ice or very cold metal directly on skin can cause cold burns, so a cloth barrier or briefer contact is common. Forum users also voice unverified nerve-damage worries.

angle.text: Forum posters press freezer-chilled spoons against the eye area to reduce puffiness. The cold narrows vessels and shifts fluid, so the under-eye looks flatter for a while. It is a home practice discussed in a few threads, with no published research.

lead: Cold spoons is a home practice in which a spoon chilled in a freezer or fridge is pressed against the skin around the eyes to reduce puffiness or bloat, so the eye area looks fresher and less swollen. People use it as a quick morning step, much like a cold compress, before going out or filming.

It borrows its logic from cold compresses. Reference material on periorbital puffiness describes a cold compress as a short-term remedy because cold narrows blood vessels, which reduces fluid leaking into the tissue and eases puffiness.[1] Puffiness around the eyes is often worst on waking because fluid shifts when a person lies flat, and other listed contributors include allergies, salt intake, lack of sleep, crying and ageing.[1]

On looksmax.org the technique is discussed in a small number of threads: one asks whether chilled spoons are legitimate for decreasing bloat, with a reply saying cold encourages blood flow and reduces swelling, and another participant recalling forum claims that ice can damage nerves. No published research has tested spoons specifically.

paras: The practice is a variation of the cold compress: a cold object is held briefly against the skin around the eyes. Cold is described as narrowing blood vessels and reducing fluid leaking into tissue, presented as a short-term effect.[1]

Periorbital puffiness has many causes, including thin skin and an enlarging fat pad under the lower eyelids with age, allergic reactions, salt and fluid retention, sleep deprivation, alcohol and fatigue, and medical conditions such as hypothyroidism. The reference notes that severe or persistent swelling may signal an underlying condition.[1] Other approaches listed for puffiness include sleeping with the head elevated, diet and lifestyle changes, and surgery.[1]

Reference material on cold therapy reports that ice applied directly to skin can cause cold burns and that serious injuries have followed excessive cooling time with powered devices.[2] The reference does not mention nerve injury for brief use, so the nerve-damage idea raised in forum discussion is not covered by that source.[2]

No studies found on cold spoons. Research on cold compression in sprains and post-surgical swelling is a different setting, and a review cited by the Wikipedia article found insufficient evidence for acute ankle sprains.[2]
